clue.text: Administration joined by northern LTA members of a militant group

blocks.note: a regime is a government or system of administration
N is the standard abbreviation for northern
the letters as printed, which must be rearranged
not accounted for by the wordplay as scanned; the printed clue may have read differently here

explanation.surface: Tennis association members join a government alongside northerners in some militant faction.
explanation.walkthrough: This clue reached us through a newspaper scan and may be garbled: no shuffle signal survives, and LTA has to be rearranged to finish the answer. The LTA is Britain's Lawn Tennis Association.
explanation.definitionFit: A regiment is a permanent army unit, so anything belonging to such a fighting body is described with this adjective.

clue.text: Blushing girl drinking cider, say?

indicators.note: 'say' asks us to speak the girl's name and take the word that matches its sound

blocks.note: Laurie Lee's memoir Cider with Rosie gives the girl who shares his cider

explanation.surface: A young woman turns pink after a drink of cider.
explanation.walkthrough: Cider with Rosie is Laurie Lee's well-known memoir of an English village childhood, so the girl with the cider is Rosie, which sounds like ROSY.
explanation.definitionFit: A blushing face turns pink, and pink-cheeked is exactly the sense of this colour adjective.

clue.text: Vivid sort of rig - chap changed it

indicators.note: a 'sort of' version is a variant, hinting the letters come in some other form
'changed' tells us the letters of the two words before it are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man has altered some colourful kind of rig, perhaps a costume or a boat's tackle.
explanation.definitionFit: A graphic account is a vivid, highly detailed one that makes a scene easy to picture.

clue.text: Used for healthy exercise - a bolus perhaps?

definitions.text: Used for healthy exercise - a bolus perhaps?

blocks.note: surface reading: a heavy ball thrown about in a gym for fitness
setter's reading: a bolus is a large pill, so a ball of medicine

explanation.walkthrough: A bolus is a big round pill, so read literally it is a ball made of medicine, while the gym object is a weighted ball for training.
explanation.definitionFit: The heavy leather ball tossed around in gyms is named for its health-giving purpose, and a large pill is literally a ball of physic.

clue.text: Novice gives pet honey by mistake

indicators.note: something put together by mistake is wrongly arranged, so the letters need sorting

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A beginner keeper accidentally feeds honey to an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A neophyte is a newcomer or beginner, originally a new convert, so it is a synonym of novice.

clue.text: Cancel article in this publication

indicators.note: 'in' places the article word inside the word for cancel

blocks.note: to annul is to cancel or declare void
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An editor announces that something will be withdrawn from the magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: The article goes in after ANNU, giving ANNU-A-L. 'This publication' is the definition: an annual is a book issued once a year.
explanation.definitionFit: An annual is a yearly book or magazine, such as a children's comic annual, so it is a kind of publication.

clue.text: Ray appears to look happy

blocks.note: first meaning: a shaft of light
second meaning: to smile broadly

explanation.surface: Someone called Ray seems cheerful.
explanation.walkthrough: Ray reads as a man's name, but it is a shaft of light.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun is a shaft of light, and as a verb it means to give a broad, radiant smile.

clue.text: Clergyman turns up in school football club

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means the word is read from bottom to top
'in' places the clergyman inside the school

blocks.note: Rev is short for Reverend, a clergyman
Eton is the famous English boarding school

explanation.surface: A vicar arrives unexpectedly at a school.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton is the famous English boarding school near Windsor; 'turns up' reads like 'arrives', but in a down clue it means read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Everton is a long-established professional soccer team based in Liverpool, England.

clue.text: Gave aid to Edward in senior government post

blocks.note: a minister holds a senior post in government
Ed is short for Edward

explanation.surface: Edward is appointed to a high Cabinet job and helps someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To minister to someone is to attend to their needs, as a nurse or priest does.

clue.text: Position onlooker has to endure to the end

blocks.note: to stand something is to put up with it
the point is the sharp end, as of a knife

explanation.surface: A spectator's view, and the need to stick it out until the finish.
explanation.definitionFit: A standpoint is the place from which an observer views something, and so a point of view or stance.

clue.text: Frenchman supplies material

blocks.note: first meaning: a common French man's first name
second meaning: a tough twilled cotton cloth

explanation.surface: A man from France provides some fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean is a typical French forename, the counterpart of John, and also the hard-wearing cotton twill from which jeans are made.

clue.text: Experts are thus familiar with a boxer's limitations

definitions.note: describes experts rather than naming a synonym: experts are people who do this
an adjective phrase for a verb phrase

blocks.note: first meaning: experienced people understand how things are done
second meaning, read literally: acquainted with the cords that bound a boxing ring

explanation.walkthrough: 'Limitations' sounds like weaknesses, but read literally it means boundaries, and a boxing ring is fenced by cords.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to understand the workings of a job, originally from sailors learning a ship's rigging.

clue.text: Smart sheikh, some might say

indicators.note: 'some might say' means the word is as certain speakers pronounce it, so we listen rather than read

blocks.note: an Arab chief, pronounced by some to rhyme with seek

explanation.surface: A well-dressed Arab leader, as people may put it.
explanation.walkthrough: Sheikh is said both to rhyme with shake and with seek; only the second gives the match, hence 'some'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chic means stylish and elegant, the same sense as smart applied to dress.

clue.text: Principal marks introductions 10 some law reports

definitions.note: the scan shows 10 where the printed clue read 'to': introductions to some law reports

blocks.note: a head is a chief or principal, as of a school
notes are written marks or jottings

explanation.surface: A head teacher grades work while drafting prefaces for legal case reports.
explanation.walkthrough: The '10' in the clue is a scanning error for 'to'.
explanation.definitionFit: In law reports a headnote is the summary placed before the judgment, stating the points the case decided.

clue.text: Writing badly of prizefighter Tom in cast

indicators.note: 'in' places the boxer's surname inside the word for cast

blocks.note: to sling is to throw or cast
Tom Cribb was a celebrated English bare-knuckle champion of the early 1800s

explanation.surface: Poor prose about a famous boxer whose arm is in plaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks like a plaster cast or a list of actors, but it is the verb throw.
explanation.definitionFit: Scribbling is hasty, untidy handwriting or careless composition, so it is writing done badly.

clue.text: Milk carriers double business, crazy!

blocks.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a business; doubled
nuts is slang for mad

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that running two firms at once is madness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Milk carriers' points to a dairy, but coconuts hold coconut milk.
explanation.definitionFit: Coconuts contain a watery juice called coconut milk, so they are fruits that hold that liquid.

clue.text: GI went mad with pain

indicators.note: letters that go mad behave wildly and fall into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An American soldier lost his mind from agony.
explanation.walkthrough: A GI is an American soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: A twinge is a sudden sharp stab of discomfort, so it is a brief kind of pain.

clue.text: S  African city before hill excellent climb

indicators.note: in a down clue, something that climbs goes upwards, so its letters are read bottom to top

blocks.note: pre- is the prefix meaning before
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor
A1 means first-rate; the 1 is read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A city in South Africa reached ahead of a fine ascent of a hill.
explanation.definitionFit: Pretoria is South Africa's administrative capital, in the province of Gauteng.

clue.text: Fish interrupts in a Zulu conference

indicators.note: something that interrupts breaks into the middle of the words that follow

blocks.note: taken as written
a dab is a small flatfish

explanation.surface: A fish intrudes on a gathering of Zulu people.
explanation.walkthrough: Indaba is a Zulu and Xhosa word that has passed into South African English.
explanation.definitionFit: An indaba is a council or meeting held among Zulu or Xhosa people, and by extension any important discussion.

clue.text: Leader of revels in sundry clubs

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter
'in' places the selected letter inside the word for sundry

blocks.note: divers is an old word for various or sundry
the opening letter of revels

explanation.surface: The organiser of a party is among various golf or night clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: Divers, stressed on the first syllable, is an old word for several; R goes inside it after the D.
explanation.definitionFit: Drivers are golf clubs with a large head, used for long shots from the tee.

clue.text: Poet's deer in retreat pursued by eagle

indicators.note: something in retreat goes backwards, so its letters run right to left

blocks.note: a hart is a male red deer
an erne is a sea eagle

explanation.surface: A writer's stag flees with an eagle chasing it.
explanation.walkthrough: A hart is a stag, and the erne, or white-tailed sea eagle, is a crossword regular; 'pursued by' means the eagle comes after the deer.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Traherne was a seventeenth-century English metaphysical writer of religious verse and prose.

clue.text: Search for the odd wise man

blocks.note: rum is British slang for odd or peculiar
a mage is a magus, a wise man or sorcerer

explanation.surface: Looking for an eccentric sage.
explanation.definitionFit: To rummage is to hunt through things untidily, so it is a way to search.

clue.text: Perhaps counsel many weary reformers

indicators.note: reformers reshape things, so the letters before it are given a new form

blocks.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a large number
taken as written

explanation.surface: Plenty of political reformers are tired out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Many' gives L, the Roman fifty, which joins the shuffled letters of weary.
explanation.definitionFit: A counsel is a barrister presenting a case in court, one example of a lawyer, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: A type of outstanding ability

blocks.note: first meaning: a very small size of printing type
second meaning: exceptionally clever or talented

explanation.surface: Someone of a remarkably gifted sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A type of' reads as 'a kind of', but 'A type' is its own definition: printers named one tiny typeface size this.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names one of the smallest old printing type sizes, and as an adjective it means dazzlingly talented.

clue.text: Frost's poetry?

blocks.note: first meaning: hoar frost formed from freezing fog
second meaning: an old spelling of rhyme, as in Coleridge's Ancient Mariner

explanation.walkthrough: Frost's looks like the American poet Robert Frost, but it is the weather word, and the poetry is the old spelling of rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a coating of ice crystals on cold surfaces, and is also the archaic spelling of verse that rhymes.

clue.text: Flog round (no game, this!)

blocks.note: first meaning: to thrash or whip
second meaning: a regular route walked by a police officer

explanation.walkthrough: The bracket warns off the shooting sense, where beaters drive game birds: here the round is a constable's patrol.
explanation.definitionFit: To beat is to strike repeatedly, and a police officer's regular patrol area is called their beat or round.

clue.text: Very cold, one month back

indicators.note: going back means reading the month word from right to left

blocks.note: the Roman numeral one
Dec is the abbreviation for December

explanation.surface: A month ago it was freezing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something chilled with frozen water is extremely cold, like iced tea or an iced drink.

clue.text: Spa hotel by aircraft or motor-boat

blocks.note: a hydro is a British hotel offering spa water treatments
a plane is an aircraft

explanation.surface: Reaching a health resort by air or by speedboat.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay alone already spells a seaplane, the older aircraft sense; 'or' adds the boat sense, which is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A hydroplane is a light, fast powered boat whose hull skims over the water surface at speed.

clue.text: Cut fuel by end of March

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: gas is a fuel
the final letter of March

explanation.surface: Fuel rations are reduced at the end of March.
explanation.definitionFit: A gash is a long deep wound, the noun sense of a cut in the skin.

clue.text: Proclamation widely read?

blocks.note: first meaning: a single printed sheet posted as a public notice
second meaning, read cryptically: a newspaper of the large page format

explanation.walkthrough: 'Widely read' suggests popularity; the question mark lets 'widely' point to the paper's wide pages instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Historically a single large printed sheet carried official announcements, and today the term names a full-size serious newspaper.
